title: Hebrews 1:1-4
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: Introduction to the Series
subpoints: Context: Preparation for the upcoming series on Hosea
Method: Using four questions to study the book of Hebrews
Goal: Viewing the Old Testament through the lens of Christ

outline.title: Question 1: Who Wrote It?
subpoints: Anonymity of the author compared to other epistles
Structure as a sermon ('word of exhortation') rather than a letter
Historical uncertainty regarding the human author (e.g., Paul, Clement of Alexandria's view)

outline.title: Characteristics of the Author
subpoints: Male gender indicated by grammatical structure in Hebrews 11:32
Second-generation believer who did not meet Jesus during His earthly ministry
Pastoral heart evidenced by frequent use of 'therefore' for application
High regard for the Word of God as living, powerful, and discerning
Likely a Greek-speaking Jewish Christian who quoted the Septuagint

summary:
This sermon introduces a three-part series on Hebrews 1:1-4, serving as a foundational lens for the subsequent study of the book of Hosea. The speaker emphasizes the necessity of reading the Old Testament through the perspective of Christ's ultimate revelation, ensuring that Christian interpretation remains distinct from purely Jewish readings. The primary objective is to introduce the book of Hebrews by posing four fundamental questions: who wrote it, to whom it was written, why it was written, and when it was written.

The first question addressed is the authorship of the epistle. Unlike other New Testament letters, Hebrews lacks a standard epistolary introduction, leading to historical uncertainty regarding its human author. While early church figures like Clement of Alexandria suggested Pauline authorship, modern scholarship generally acknowledges the anonymity of the writer. The text notes that the structure of the book resembles a sermon or 'word of exhortation' rather than a formal letter, a term used in Acts 13 to describe apostolic preaching.

Despite the unknown name, the text reveals significant characteristics of the author. Grammatical evidence in Hebrews 11:32 indicates the author was male. The author is identified as a second-generation Christian who did not personally know Jesus during His earthly ministry but was saved under the ministry of the first generation. The author demonstrates a strong pastoral heart, frequently using the word 'therefore' to apply doctrine to daily life. Furthermore, the author exhibits a high regard for the Word of God, viewing it as living, powerful, and capable of discerning the heart, while quoting extensively from the Greek translation of the Old Testament, suggesting a Greek-speaking Jewish Christian background.
